Question 1

When overloading a function, what must be true?

  • A. The names should be different with different number and/or types of parameters.
  • B. None of the choices are correct
  • C. The names should be different with the same number and/or types of parameters.
  • D. The names should be the same with different number and/or types of parameters.
  • E. The names should be the same with the same number and/or types of parameters.

Source

  • Mock exam 4 · Question 15

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare names and parameter signatures before considering return types or access modifiers.

Study-guide sections

OOP12 · Method overloading and compile-time selection

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP12 · Method overloading and compile-time selection

Correct answer: D — The names should be the same with different number and/or types of parameters.

Overloads retain the method name and change parameter count or parameter types; return type alone cannot distinguish them.

Evidence in the complete study note

Overloaded methods share a name but have different parameter types, counts or type order. Return type alone is insufficient in Java and C++. Overloads can also arise through inherited methods; “same class only” is a teaching simplification. f(int), f(double) and f(int,int) are distinct, but changing a parameter name does not create an overload.OOP12

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Different names do not overload one function

B · incorrect — D satisfies the overloading rule, so the statement that none of the choices is correct is false.

C · incorrect — Different names define separate methods

D · correct — Same name plus different parameter list meets the definition

E · incorrect — Same name and same parameter signature cannot distinguish overloads

Question 3

Which generation of programming languages stated for high-level languages like C++, Java, Python?

  • A. 2nd generation
  • B. 3rd generation
  • C. 4th generation
  • D. None of the above

Sources

  • National Exit Exam practice questions · Question 14

  • Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 84

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Separate language-generation classification, translation strategy and portability assumptions.

Study-guide sections

OOP39 · Language classifications and portability

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP39 · Language classifications and portability

Correct answer: B — Third generation.

OOP39 explicitly places general-purpose high-level languages such as C++, Java and Python in the third generation. This taxonomy concerns historical language classification, not whether a language is object oriented or interpreted. Thus the third-generation option applies to all the examples named in the question.

Evidence in the complete study note

Under the conventional introductory generation taxonomy, general-purpose high-level languages such as C++, Java, Python and Perl are third generation. The taxonomy is separate from object orientation and from compilation versus interpretation. Java source normally compiles to JVM bytecode, and a compatible JVM plus libraries supports portability across systems.OOP39

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Second generation is not the category assigned to these general-purpose high-level examples in OOP39.

B · correct — Third generation is the explicit conventional category assigned to C++, Java and Python.

C · incorrect — Fourth generation does not match the explicit third-generation classification of the named examples.

D · incorrect — The third-generation option is present, so none of the above cannot be correct.

Question 5

What is the output of the following Java fragment code? int n = 6, m = 15, p = 3; n -= m; n *= p; System.out.print(n);

  • A. 27
  • B. 3
  • C. 24
  • D. -27

Sources

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · Question 21-1

  • National Computer Science Exit Exam · Question 77

  • National Computer Science Exit Exam

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam

  • Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 76

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Respect operator grouping and operand types, then trace each operation in evaluation order.

Study-guide sections

OOP23 · Expressions: numbers, bits and text output

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP23 · Expressions: numbers, bits and text output

Correct answer: D — -27.

Start with n=6. The subtraction assignment n-=m computes 6-15, leaving n=-9. The multiplication assignment then uses that updated value: -9*3=-27. OOP23 includes this exact trace. The sign cannot become positive because only subtraction followed by multiplication by positive three occurs.

Evidence in the complete study note

Java evaluates operands left to right while respecting precedence. With n=6,m=15,p=3, n-=m then n*=p leaves -27.OOP23

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — 27 discards the negative sign produced when 15 is subtracted from 6.

B · incorrect — Three is the unchanged multiplier p, not the updated value of n that is printed.

C · incorrect — 24 does not follow either the subtraction result -9 or its subsequent multiplication by 3.

D · correct — The ordered updates yield n=-9 and then n=-27, which System.out.print outputs.

Question 6

What is the output of the following Java fragment code? int[] list = new int[4]; int sum = 0; for(int i = 0; i < list.length; i++) { list[i] = i * 3; sum += list[i]; } System.out.print(sum);

  • A. 18
  • B. 6
  • C. 3
  • D. 36

Sources

  • National Computer Science Exit Exam · Question 42

  • National Computer Science Exit Exam

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace every element or API argument and distinguish copying values from aliasing a reference.

Study-guide sections

OOP27 · Array algorithms, sort and copy APIs

OOP26 · Arrays: creation, bounds and ragged rows

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP27 · Array algorithms, sort and copy APIs

OOP26 · Arrays: creation, bounds and ragged rows

Correct answer: A — 18.

The length-four array is visited at indices 0,1,2,3. Assigning i*3 stores 0,3,6,9. Starting sum at zero and adding each element gives 18, exactly the example in OOP27. The loop processes four elements, not merely the first one or an uninitialized default array.

Evidence in the complete study note

For int[] a=new int[4], setting a[i]=i*3 and accumulating yields 0+3+6+9=18.OOP27
Valid indices are 0..a.length-1; an invalid access throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.OOP26

Choice by choice

A · correct — All four assigned elements contribute: 0+3+6+9 equals the printed sum 18.

B · incorrect — Six is one element’s value, not the sum after all four iterations.

C · incorrect — Three is the element assigned at index 1, rather than the full accumulator result.

D · incorrect — 36 doubles the actual total; each of the four elements is added only once.

Question 7

Consider the following program: import java.util.Scanner; public class Test { public static void main(String[] args) { Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in); System.out.println("enter choice"); int choice = scanner.nextInt(); switch (choice) { case 1: System.out.println("Hello"); case 2: System.out.println("you"); break; default: System.out.println("welcome"); } System.out.println("Goodbye"); } } After entering 1, what lines are printed following the initial “enter choice” prompt? Preserve letter case.

  • A. Hello You welcome
  • B. Hello You Welcome Goodbye
  • C. Hello Goodbye
  • D. Hello you Goodbye

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam collection · Question 85

  • Computer Science model exam collection

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace condition tests, control transfers and printing as separate steps.

Study-guide sections

OOP25 · Control flow traces and exact printing

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP25 · Control flow traces and exact printing

Correct answer: D — Hello you Goodbye

Input 1 selects case 1, which prints Hello but has no break. Execution falls through to case 2 and prints you. Its break exits the switch before default, so welcome does not print. The final println outside the switch prints Goodbye. The requested output excludes the initial input prompt and preserves exact letter case.

Evidence in the complete study note

break exits the loop; continue skips its remaining body and then runs a for update. Traditional colon-style switch labels fall through without break. Choice 1 printing Hello then case 2 printing you and breaking is followed by Goodbye outside the switch; default is skipped.OOP25

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — This incorrectly includes welcome and omits the final Goodbye.

B · incorrect — Default is skipped after case 2 breaks, so this includes an extra line.

C · incorrect — Fall-through executes case 2, so omitting you is wrong.

D · correct — The exact post-prompt lines are Hello, you and Goodbye.

Question 8

Which one of the following is false regarding Exceptions in Java?

  • A. We cannot create our own exception classes by extending Exception class
  • B. Exception class describes errors caused by your program and external circumstances
  • C. Runtime Exception class describes programming errors such as bad casting and numeric errors
  • D. All Java exception classes inherit directly or indirectly from Throwable class

Sources

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 35

  • Mock exam 4 · Question 30

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Separate source errors from runtime exceptions and determine the hierarchy and checked obligation.

Study-guide sections

OOP29 · Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP29 · Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

Correct answer: A — We cannot create our own exception classes by extending Exception class

The prohibition on user-defined exceptions is false: an exception class can extend Throwable or a subclass. Its examples describe input, file and resource failures and runtime programming bugs.

Evidence in the complete study note

Throwable is the root of throwable values, with Exception and Error branches. RuntimeException and Error subclasses are unchecked; other throwable classes are checked. IOException, FileNotFoundException and SQLException are standard checked examples. ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ClassCastException and array bounds exceptions are unchecked. A missing semicolon or undeclared variable is a compile-time source error, not a checked exception.OOP29
A custom exception can extend Exception or RuntimeException.OOP29

Choice by choice

A · correct — Contradicts the explicit permission to define exception classes

B · incorrect — Consistent with user, programmer and resource failures

C · incorrect — Consistent with runtime programming bugs, though individual bad-cast examples are not enumerated

D · incorrect — Matches the Throwable ancestry rule

OOP01 · Objects, classes and responsibilities

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP01 · Objects, classes and responsibilities

Correct answer: D — Behavior

getArea and getPerimeter describe operations performed by a rectangle, so they are behavior rather than its stored state.

Evidence in the complete study note

An object has identity, state and behavior. State is stored in fields; behavior is provided by methods. A Rectangle object may hold width and height and answer getArea() or getPerimeter(). Two objects can have equal fields and still be distinct objects. A class defines their common structure and behavior; an object is a particular instance.OOP01

Question 10

Which one of the following is false about abstract classes and abstract methods?

  • A. We can create instances of abstract classes using the new operator
  • B. Implementation of abstract methods is provided by the subclasses
  • C. A class that contains abstract methods must be defined as abstract
  • D. Abstract methods are defined without implementation in the superclass

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check whether a class is concrete and whether every inherited abstract contract has an implementation.

Study-guide sections

OOP18 · Abstract classes and concrete implementations

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP18 · Abstract classes and concrete implementations

Correct answer: A — We can create instances of abstract classes using the new operator

The abstract-class example permits a concrete method but forbids new A(); subclasses supply the body for callme(). Thus instantiation is the false claim.

Evidence in the complete study note

An abstract class cannot be directly instantiated but can define fields, constructors, abstract methods and concrete methods. It need not contain an abstract method. An abstract method has no body; abstract and final conflict because an operation cannot require overriding while forbidding it.OOP18
A concrete subclass must provide or inherit implementations of all required abstract methods; otherwise it must itself be abstract.OOP18

Choice by choice

A · correct — Direct new instantiation is forbidden

B · incorrect — B supplies the implementation of callme in the example

C · incorrect — An abstract method is an unimplemented requirement of an abstract class in this model

OOP24 · Increment order and the character-space trap

while and for pre-test and may execute zero times; do-while post-tests and executes once.OOP25

Question 13

Which valid Java declaration reproduces a ragged table with first row 12, -9, 8; second row 7, 14; and third row -32, -1, 0? The second row has two elements, not a third element containing zero.

  • A. double[][] table = {12, -9, 8, 7, 14, -32, -1, 0};
  • B. double[][] table = { {12, -9, 8}, {7,14,0}, {-32,-1,0}};
  • C. double[][] table = { { 12,-9,8} {7,14} {-32,-1,0}};
  • D. double[][] table = { {12, -9, 8},{7, 14},{-32, -1, 0} };

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 29

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check declared dimensions, initializer shape, fixed length and zero-based index bounds.

Study-guide sections

OOP26 · Arrays: creation, bounds and ragged rows

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP26 · Arrays: creation, bounds and ragged rows

Correct answer: D — Use rows {12,-9,8}, {7,14}, {-32,-1,0}.

Java represents a two-dimensional array as an array of row arrays, so the rows may have different lengths. The source table has lengths 3, 2 and 3. D supplies exactly those rows with comma-separated nested initializers. B is syntactically valid but adds an unwanted middle-row zero. A supplies scalar values where row arrays are needed, and C omits commas between its row initializers.

Evidence in the complete study note

int[] a=new int[5]; and int a[]={1,2,3}; are valid. int[] a={}; creates a zero-length array; explicit new is unnecessary in a declaration initializer.OOP26
Valid indices are 0..a.length-1; an invalid access throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Java two-dimensional arrays are arrays of arrays and may be ragged: {{12,-9,8},{7,14},{-32,-1,0}} has row lengths 3,2,3. Java does not expose a portable physical contiguity guarantee, so a language-level answer should not rely on raw addresses.OOP26

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — The declared double[][] requires row-array elements; a flat list of numeric scalars does not supply them.

B · incorrect — Its second row contains an extra zero and therefore does not match the two-element row.

C · incorrect — Missing commas between the row initializers make this declaration syntactically incorrect.

D · correct — Its nested comma-separated rows match the required values and lengths 3, 2 and 3.

OOP07 · Static members, static blocks and final

Correct answers (select all): A, C — The PI field of a circle class; A method that calculates the hypotenuse of a right-angle triangle class

PI is one shared mathematical constant, so a static final field suits it. A hypotenuse utility that uses only parameters also needs no current object and can be static. Question 16

What is the output of the following Java 17 code? class FinalExam{ int num1; public FinalExam() { num1 = 4; } void display() { System.out.println(num1) ; } } class Final1 extends FinalExam{ int num=3; public Final1() { this(5); num1 = num; } public Final1(int num) { this.num = num * num; } } public class Main{ public static void main(String[] args){ Final1 f = new Final1(); f.display(); } }

  • A. 4
  • B. 25
  • C. 12
  • D. 20

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 32

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace constructor delegation and initialization in the specified Java version.

Study-guide sections

OOP10 · Constructor chaining and initialization order

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP10 · Constructor chaining and initialization order

Correct answer: B — 25

Constructing Final1 first runs the parent constructor, setting num1 to 4. Subclass initialization sets num to 3. The delegated Final1(int) body receives 5 and sets num to 25. Control returns to the no-argument body, which assigns num1=num, replacing 4 with 25. display then prints inherited num1. Consistent subclass and constructor names make this an executable Java 17 trace.

Evidence in the complete study note

Under Java 17 rules, an explicit this(args) or super(args) invocation must be the first constructor statement. this invokes another constructor in the same class; super invokes the immediate superclass constructor. A constructor cannot explicitly invoke both. If there is no explicit delegation, an implicit super() is inserted; a matching accessible no-argument parent constructor must exist.OOP10
Trace parent construction first, then subclass field initializers and instance blocks in order, then the relevant subclass constructor body. With consistent class and constructor names and this(5) chaining in the FinalExam example, the parent sets num1=4, the subclass initializes num=3, this(5) sets num=25, and the no-arg body sets num1=num, leaving 25.OOP10

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — 4 is the parent’s initial num1 value, overwritten by the no-argument subclass body.

B · correct — The delegated constructor sets num=25 and the caller copies it to num1.

C · incorrect — 12 is not produced by squaring the delegated argument or by the assignments.

D · incorrect — 20 is not produced by the constructor chain.

Question 18

An accessible parent declares public abstract int value(); and its direct child is non-abstract with no inherited implementation of that method. What must the child do?

  • A. A child must override an abstract method inherited from its parent by defining a method with the same signature and same return type
  • B. A child must define an additional method similar to the one inherited from its parent by defining a method with the same signature and different return type.
  • C. Achild must not define any method with the same signature as the parent's abstract method.
  • D. A non-abstract child must define an abstract method with the same signature and same return type as the parent's abstract method.
  • E. All of the above

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 34

  • Mock exam 3 · Question 18

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check whether a class is concrete and whether every inherited abstract contract has an implementation.

Study-guide sections

OOP18 · Abstract classes and concrete implementations

OOP14 · Overriding and restrictions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP18 · Abstract classes and concrete implementations

OOP14 · Overriding and restrictions

Correct answer: A — A child must override an abstract method inherited from its parent by defining a method with the same signature and same return type

A concrete child must implement every outstanding abstract method. Here the inherited contract has no parameters and a primitive int return, so the child must supply a public concrete implementation of that same signature and return type. The covariant reference-return exception does not apply to primitive int. A different return type, refusing to implement the method, or declaring it abstract leaves the concrete-class requirement unsatisfied.

Evidence in the complete study note

A concrete subclass must provide or inherit implementations of all required abstract methods; otherwise it must itself be abstract. If parent declares abstract String welcome(), a String welcome() implementation is required; int welcome() is incompatible, and welcome(int) merely adds an overload. A valid class can contain both the required implementation and an unrelated overload.OOP18
A subclass overrides an eligible inherited instance method with the same signature and a compatible return type; a covariant reference return may be a subtype. Visibility cannot become more restrictive, and checked exceptions cannot be broadened incompatibly.OOP14

Choice by choice

A · correct — A concrete matching no-argument int implementation, with the required public access, satisfies the inherited contract.

B · incorrect — A different return type cannot implement this primitive int-returning contract.

C · incorrect — Omitting a matching implementation leaves an abstract obligation in the concrete child.

D · incorrect — An abstract declaration supplies no implementation and cannot satisfy the concrete child’s obligation.

E · incorrect — B, C and D fail the stated implementation requirement, so the aggregate cannot be correct.

Study-guide references

OOP13 · Inheritance and useful relationships

OOP19 · Interfaces: contracts and modern Java

Correct answer: C — A child class can extend just one parent and can implement zero or more interfaces.

A Java class can extend one class and implement multiple interfaces.

Evidence in the complete study note

class Dog extends Animal declares a subclass/derived/child of a superclass/base/parent. A class extends one direct class and can implement multiple interfaces. Single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance mean one parent, a chain, and several children of one parent. Java does not permit class Dog extends Animal,Mammal.OOP13
A class can extend a superclass and implement zero or more interfaces.OOP19

B · incorrect — Artificially limits interfaces to one

Question 20

What will be the output of the program? try { int x = 0; int y = 5 / x; } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("Exception"); } catch (ArithmeticException ae) { System.out.println("Arithmetic Exception"); } System.out.println("finished");

  • A. Arithmetic Exception
  • B. finished
  • C. Exception
  • D. Compilation fails.

Source

  • Mock exam 4 · Question 26

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check the thrown type and catch order before tracing propagation or handler output.

Study-guide sections

OOP30 · throw, throws and catch selection

OOP29 · Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP30 · throw, throws and catch selection

OOP29 · Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

Correct answer: D — Compilation fails because the subtype catch is unreachable.

Exception is caught before its subclass ArithmeticException. OOP30 says that a general catch before a subtype catch makes the latter unreachable and prevents compilation. The program therefore never executes the division or either print statement. Reasoning about which handler would run cannot bypass this compile-time restriction.

Evidence in the complete study note

Catch blocks are considered in source order. Place FileNotFoundException before IOException and IOException before Exception; a general catch before a subtype catch makes that later handler unreachable and prevents compilation.OOP30
Throwable is the root of throwable values, with Exception and Error branches. RuntimeException and Error subclasses are unchecked; other throwable classes are checked. IOException, FileNotFoundException and SQLException are standard checked examples. ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ClassCastException and array bounds exceptions are unchecked.OOP29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — The ArithmeticException handler is unreachable at compile time, so it cannot print its message.

B · incorrect — Compilation fails before execution; the statement following the catches never prints finished.

C · incorrect — Although Exception could catch this runtime type, the illegal later catch prevents any execution.

D · correct — The earlier Exception catch subsumes ArithmeticException, making the later handler unreachable and the program uncompilable.

Question 23

Public classes A, B and C are in three different packages, with C extending B and B extending A. From code declared inside C, accessing fields through this, which is the complete access set? Assume ordinary instance fields with distinct names, accessible public declaring types, and no hiding.

  • A. All fields declared in C, and only accessible inherited protected and public fields from A and B
  • B. Protected, default and public data only in C and B.
  • C. Any data in C and only public data in A and B.
  • D. Protected, default and public data only in C.

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · Question 8

  • University of Gondar model exam · Question 8

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Locate the accessing code, declaring type, package and receiver before applying visibility rules.

Study-guide sections

OOP08 · Access control and package boundaries

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP08 · Access control and package boundaries

Correct answer: A — All fields declared in C, and only accessible inherited protected and public fields from A and B

Code inside C can access C’s own fields, including private ones. Across package boundaries it can also access inherited public and protected fields through its own inherited context, here represented by this. It cannot access package-private or private ancestor fields directly. Consequently A gives the complete set; the public-only choice is incomplete because qualifying protected inherited access is also permitted.

Evidence in the complete study note

For ordinary members: private restricts access to the declaring class/nest; no modifier grants package access; protected grants same-package access plus qualified subclass access; public is widest, provided the declaring type itself is accessible. Top-level classes/interfaces may be public or package-private, not protected/private. Member types have additional visibility possibilities.OOP08
Across packages, a subclass accessing a protected instance member must do so through its own inherited context or an appropriate subclass-typed receiver, not any arbitrary superclass object.OOP08

Choice by choice

A · correct — This includes C’s own fields and the inherited public/protected access permitted through this.

B · incorrect — Package-private ancestor fields in different packages are not accessible, and A’s inherited access is omitted.

C · incorrect — This omits accessible inherited protected fields and therefore is not the complete set.

D · incorrect — This omits C’s own private access and permitted inherited ancestor access.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP11 · Methods, getters and setters

OOP16 · this, super, fields and static hiding

Correct answers (select all): A, C — Methodname(); Objectname.methodname()

An unqualified call inside a suitable instance context uses implicit this, so Methodname() is valid. An object-qualified call explicitly supplies the receiver and is also valid. A type name alone cannot invoke a non-static method without an object. The final form lacks invocation parentheses and therefore does not invoke a method. These are deliberate syntax alternatives under the stated placeholder meanings.

Evidence in the complete study note

A method has modifiers, return type, name, parameter list and body: public int getAge(){return age;}. A void method returns no value. Parameters name the inputs in the declaration; arguments supply values at a call. An instance method can be invoked as object.method(), or with an implicit this inside suitable instance context.OOP11
Java this and super are unavailable as current-instance references in static context.OOP16

Choice by choice

A · correct — The unqualified call uses implicit this in the stated instance context.

B · incorrect — A class name alone does not provide the required instance receiver.

C · correct — The object-qualified call supplies the instance receiver.

D · incorrect — Without parentheses this form does not perform a method invocation.

Question 25

In Java, Base declares an eligible instance method m(), Sub overrides it, and an object’s exact runtime class is Sub. Inside an instance method declared in Sub, what happens on an unqualified call m()? Assume no further subclass or explicit super call.

  • A. The Compiler will choose randomly the method to be executed
  • B. It will always refer to the version of that method defined by the subclass
  • C. Compile time error will occur
  • D. It will always refer to the version of that method defined by the superclass

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · Question 10

  • University of Gondar model exam · Question 10

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check what compiles from the declared type, then select behavior from the actual runtime class.

Study-guide sections

OOP15 · Dynamic dispatch: declared type versus actual type

OOP16 · this, super, fields and static hiding

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP15 · Dynamic dispatch: declared type versus actual type

OOP16 · this, super, fields and static hiding

Correct answer: B — It will always refer to the version of that method defined by the subclass

The unqualified invocation uses the current Sub object as receiver. Since m is an eligible overridden instance method and the exact runtime class is Sub, dynamic dispatch selects Sub’s implementation. The compiler does not choose randomly, and the valid declaration produces no compilation error. An explicit super.m() would request the parent version, but that is excluded by the specified call expression.

Evidence in the complete study note

For Animal a=new Dog(), Animal is the declared type and Dog the actual type. The declared type determines which member operations compile. If fetch() exists only in Dog, a.fetch() fails compilation. For an eligible overridden sound(), a.sound() invokes Dog.sound() at runtime.OOP15
An unqualified instance call may dispatch dynamically; an explicit super call is different.OOP16

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Dispatch follows the language’s receiver and overriding rules, not random choice.

B · correct — The exact Sub receiver dispatches the ordinary call to Sub.m().

C · incorrect — The stated accessible, eligible declaration and call compile.

D · incorrect — The superclass version would require a different dispatch situation such as explicit super.m().

Study-guide references

OOP08 · Access control and package boundaries

Correct answer: A — A private member of a class cannot be accessed by the methods of the same class

Private visibility is class-only, so methods of the declaring class can access that member. Public is world-visible; protected includes subclasses.

Evidence in the complete study note

For ordinary members: private restricts access to the declaring class/nest; no modifier grants package access; protected grants same-package access plus qualified subclass access; public is widest, provided the declaring type itself is accessible. Top-level classes/interfaces may be public or package-private, not protected/private. Member types have additional visibility possibilities.OOP08

Correct answer: C — Compiler error.

The for condition is integer literal 0, whereas OOP06 explicitly says for(...;0;...) is invalid in Java. The doubled quotes around Hello are another source syntax defect. boolean does not convert to or from numeric truth values; if(0) and for(...;0;...) are invalid.OOP06
An identifier is a programmer-chosen name for an entity such as a class, method or variable. A reserved keyword has a language-defined role and cannot be used as an ordinary identifier. A literal writes a value directly, such as an integer, floating-point number, quoted character, quoted string or Boolean value.OOP-S01
A while header is while(condition). A basic for header is for(initialization; condition; update). A do-while statement places its condition after the body. An if selects its true branch or, when present, its else branch; only the selected branch executes.OOP-S03

D · incorrect — The program fails translation before execution, so the relevant failure is not a runtime exception.

Correct answer: C — 40.

D · incorrect — 48 requires g to become 6, but the single increment changes it only from 4 to 5.

Question 51

What will this program print when run on Java 17? class area { public static void main(String args[]) { double r, pi, a; r = 9.8; pi = 3.14; a = pi * r * r; System.out.println(a); } }

  • A. 301.5656
  • B. 301
  • C. 301.56
  • D. 301.57

  • Object-Oriented Programming practice questions · Question 23

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Read the cited conceptual rules, state the model, and apply them before comparing the alternatives.

Study-guide sections

OOP-S02 · Java 17 floating-point evaluation and printed doubles

Additional reading: Java SE 17 JLS — Floating-point Expressions and Multiplicative Operators↗

Additional reading: Java SE 17 — Double.toString(double)↗

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP-S02 · Java 17 floating-point evaluation and printed doubles

Correct answer: A — 301.5656

Java groups pi * r * r as (pi * r) * r and rounds each double multiplication using binary64 arithmetic. The resulting value has hexadecimal representation 0x1.2d90cb295e9e2p+8. Java 17’s standard conversion prints that value as 301.5656, followed by println’s line terminator. The supplementary Oracle rules establish the precise arithmetic and text conversion; no separate decimal-place formatting is applied.

Evidence in the complete study note

Java 17 float uses IEEE 754 binary32, and double uses binary64. Successive multiplications group from left to right. Each floating-point operation rounds to its representable result, using nearest-value rounding with ties to even; regrouping a product can change its result.OOP-S02
PrintStream.print(double) converts the stored value through String.valueOf and Double.toString. For finite nonzero magnitudes from 0.001 inclusive to 10000000 exclusive, the standard decimal form uses at least one fractional digit and only the further digits needed to distinguish the value from adjacent doubles. println(double) also adds a line terminator. This is not fixed-decimal-place formatting.OOP-S02

Additional authoritative reference

Successive multiplications group from left to right. Java 17 double operations use binary64 with each product rounded to the nearest representable value; applying these rules gives 0x1.2d90cb295e9e2p+8 for this expression.

Java SE 17 JLS — Floating-point Expressions and Multiplicative Operators↗

For a finite double of this magnitude the decimal representation uses only the fractional digits needed to distinguish the value from adjacent doubles. The computed value is the same binary64 value as literal 301.5656, and this decimal is its distinguishing representation.

Java SE 17 — Double.toString(double)↗

Choice by choice

A · correct — 301.5656 is the standard Java 17 printed representation of the computed double.

B · incorrect — There is no integer conversion that discards the fractional part.

C · incorrect — The program does not truncate or format the result to two decimal places.

D · incorrect — The program does not round its displayed output to two decimal places.

Correct answer: C — 13.

OOP23 · Expressions: numbers, bits and text output

Correct answer: C — 14.

The AND produces 11&9 = 1011&1001 = 1001, or 9. XOR with 3 gives 1001^0011 = 1010, or 10. OR with 12 then gives 1010|1100 = 1110, or 14. OOP23 explicitly provides this chain; these are integer bitwise operations, not Boolean short-circuit operations.

D · incorrect — Eight omits bits set by the final OR of binary 1010 and 1100.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP-S03 · Expression results, assignment and control headers

Correct answer: D — x becomes 8.

The last statement assigns 8 to z, then that same assigned value to y and then x. The earlier x=0 and y=1 values are overwritten, and no addition takes place. This follows assignment’s value propagation rather than the left-to-right operand arithmetic discussed in OOP23. The final stored value of x is 8.

B · incorrect — One is y’s earlier value, which is also overwritten before x receives the chain’s result.

C · incorrect — The statement performs assignments, not addition of the earlier y value to 8.

D · correct — The chain assigns 8 to z, then y and x, leaving x equal to 8.

Correct answer: C — while

A while loop tests its condition before every possible execution and has a condition-only header. A for loop is also a pre-test loop, but its ordinary header has initialization, condition and update clauses. A do-while loop tests after its body and therefore runs at least once. The added header and timing distinctions make while the unique match rather than relying on repetition alone.

D · incorrect — The valid new-array expression in OOP26 demonstrates dynamic allocation, so none is false.

Question 85

Which is an inherent property of Java arrays? Here “Code Optimization” means a guarantee that merely introducing an array makes every algorithm run faster.

  • B. Random access
  • C. Size No-Limit
  • D. Both A and B

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP27 · Array algorithms, sort and copy APIs

OOP26 · Arrays: creation, bounds and ragged rows

OOP03 · Create objects and distinguish references from instances

Correct answer: B — Random access is the concrete array advantage.

Arrays provide indexed random access, so B states the inherent capability. They have a fixed length after creation and are bounded by implementation limits and available resources, so unlimited size is false. An array is a storage structure, not a guarantee that every algorithm becomes faster: allocating an unused array cannot improve a computation that does not need it. A therefore fails the stated guarantee, and combining it with B does not make D correct.

Evidence in the complete study note

Random access is the reliable array advantage; size is bounded by implementation/resources, not unlimited.OOP27
Array objects have fixed length after creation, although the reference may be reassigned.OOP26
Student s=new Student(); allocates and initializes an instance.OOP03

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — The stated universal speedup does not follow from array storage; adding an unused allocation does not improve the algorithm’s required computation.

B · correct — Indexed random access is a direct array capability.

C · incorrect — Array length is fixed after creation and constrained by implementation limits and resources.

D · incorrect — This conjunction includes the false universal optimization guarantee, even though random access itself is true.

Question 86

OOP26 · Arrays: creation, bounds and ragged rows

OOP27 · Array algorithms, sort and copy APIs

Correct answer: B — Sequential

Java arrays expose a logical sequence of indices starting at zero and ending at length minus one. Sequential describes that order. Random access describes the ability to choose an index directly, not a random logical ordering of elements or a portable physical-memory arrangement. Binary search is an algorithm rather than an ordering description. The revised question therefore tests index semantics without assuming exposed physical contiguity.

C · incorrect — Combining access capability with ordering does not give the precise ordering term requested.

D · incorrect — Binary search is an algorithm, not the array’s logical index order.

Therefore java.util is the package category supported for the named utility examples, rather than the language, networking or UI alternatives.

Evidence in the complete study note

Calendar and Date are classes in java.util; Collection is an interface in that package. java.util also contains Arrays and Scanner. java.net supplies networking facilities; java.awt supplies the Button and Checkbox UI controls described in the package overview.OOP-S04
java.lang is implicitly imported; java.util supplies utilities; java.io supplies I/O; java.awt includes Button and Checkbox.OOP28

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — java.lang supplies core language facilities; the utility package identified here is java.util.

B · incorrect — java.net is the networking alternative, not the utility package identified in OOP28.

C · incorrect — java.awt contains AWT UI controls, rather than the utility facilities requested by the question.

D · correct — java.util is the note’s explicit utility-package mapping for the class/interface examples in the stem.

Question 97

An accessible class declares an ordinary field. Which offered modifier choices permit another unrelated class in the same package to access that field directly? Choose the most complete answer; this asks about member modifiers, not top-level class modifiers.

  • A. Public
  • B. Protected
  • C. No Modifier
  • D. All of the mentioned

Adapted from

  • Object-Oriented Programming practice questions · Question 74

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Locate the accessing code, declaring type, package and receiver before applying visibility rules.

Study-guide sections

OOP08 · Access control and package boundaries

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP08 · Access control and package boundaries

Correct answer: D — All of the mentioned

For ordinary members, public allows access, protected includes same-package access, and no modifier grants package access. All three listed choices therefore permit the unrelated same-package client to access the field. This does not claim that protected is legal on a top-level class, and class accessibility alone would not expose a private field. Under the explicitly member-level scope, D is the complete selection.

Evidence in the complete study note

For ordinary members: private restricts access to the declaring class/nest; no modifier grants package access; protected grants same-package access plus qualified subclass access; public is widest, provided the declaring type itself is accessible.OOP08
protected therefore does not mean “subclasses only”: unrelated classes in the same package also have access.OOP08

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Public permits the access, but this is only one of the three valid modifier choices.

B · incorrect — Protected includes same-package access, but this option alone is incomplete.

C · incorrect — No modifier grants package access, but this option alone is incomplete.

D · correct — All three listed member-modifier choices permit the specified same-package access.

Question 99

Which of the following is false statement about package in java?

  • A. Packages are used for preventing naming conflicts
  • B. Providing controlled access: protected and default have package level access control.
  • C. Packages cannot be considered as data encapsulation
  • D. Both B and C

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP28 · Packages, imports and command-line tools

OOP08 · Access control and package boundaries

OOP02 · Four principles and the difference between hiding and abstraction

Correct answer: C — The claim that packages cannot support encapsulation is false.

OOP28 says packages organize names and control access, while OOP08 defines package access and same-package protected access. These mechanisms can hide implementation types or members behind permitted boundaries, so C’s categorical denial is false. A and B describe real package roles. D incorrectly includes the true package-access statement B among the false claims.

Evidence in the complete study note

Packages organize names and control access; hierarchical spelling does not grant special access between a package and its subpackages.OOP28
For ordinary members: private restricts access to the declaring class/nest; no modifier grants package access; protected grants same-package access plus qualified subclass access; public is widest, provided the declaring type itself is accessible.OOP08
protected therefore does not mean “subclasses only”: unrelated classes in the same package also have access.OOP08
Information hiding keeps implementation decisions behind a stable interface.OOP02

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Organizing names into packages supports avoiding naming conflicts, so this is a true purpose rather than the false claim.

B · incorrect — Default access is package access, and protected also grants same-package access; the statement is true.

C · correct — Packages control access and can hide implementation types or members, contradicting this categorical denial of encapsulation.

D · incorrect — B is supported by the access rules, so both B and C cannot be classified as false.

Question 100

For a Java naming hierarchy such as p and p.q, what is the specific conventional term for packages such as p.q relative to p?

OOP28 · Packages, imports and command-line tools

Correct answer: D — Subpackages.

The conventional term for p.q relative to p is subpackage. This is a naming hierarchy, not a lexical enclosing scope: the parent’s import does not automatically import types from the subpackage, and their related names grant no special member access. Packages is only the broad category. The util qualifier would restrict the answer to a particular package family instead of naming the general relationship.

Correct answers (select all): A, C, D — public static; public final; static final

OOP29 · Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP29 · Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

Correct answer: A — Exceptions are thrown at runtime; checked obligations are checked at compile time.

OOP29 explains that checked does not mean an exception occurs during compilation. The compiler verifies catch-or-declare obligations; an actual exception throw occurs during program execution. Therefore Run Time is the correct occurrence answer. Compile-time syntax or name errors are a different category and do not make Java exceptions occur at any arbitrary stage.

Evidence in the complete study note

A missing semicolon or undeclared variable is a compile-time source error, not a checked exception.OOP29
Checked does not mean the exception occurs at compile time: the compiler checks an obligation to catch or declare it, while an actual throw occurs at runtime.OOP29

Choice by choice

A · correct — An actual exception throw occurs during execution, as OOP29 explicitly states.

B · incorrect — Any time conflates runtime throwing with compile-time checking and source errors.

C · incorrect — Compilation checks obligations or reports source errors; it is not when the described program throws an exception.

D · incorrect — Run Time is offered and is the supported occurrence stage, so none is false.

Correct answer: B — java.lang.Exception belongs to java.lang.

The base Exception class belongs to java.lang, which is implicitly imported. Its place in the Throwable hierarchy does not determine the package of every subclass: I/O-specific subclasses may belong to java.io while the base remains java.lang.Exception. java.util contains utility types, and java.file is not the package of this class. Thus B supplies the correct package.

Evidence in the complete study note

The base Exception class is java.lang.Exception. It does not belong to java.io merely because some subclasses represent I/O failures. Package membership and position in an inheritance hierarchy are separate facts.OOP-S04
Throwable is the root of throwable values, with Exception and Error branches.OOP29
java.lang is implicitly imported; java.util supplies utilities; java.io supplies I/O; java.awt includes Button and Checkbox.OOP28

Additional authoritative reference

The Exception class is declared in the java.lang package.

Java SE17 API: java.lang.Exception↗

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — The official API places Exception in java.lang, not the proposed java.file package.

B · correct — The official Java SE17 API explicitly identifies Exception as a java.lang class.

C · incorrect — Specific I/O exceptions do not relocate the Exception base class from java.lang into java.io.

D · incorrect — java.util provides utility types, while the authoritative API places Exception in java.lang.

Question 121

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP34 · Legacy applets and lifecycle questions

Correct answer: A — start.

OOP34 says init initializes once and start follows initialization and resumes activity. Thus start is the lifecycle method called after init under the historical host model. stop suspends activity, destroy cleans up before unloading, and paint draws content; none states the next lifecycle stage after initialization.

A · correct — start follows initialization and resumes applet activity, exactly matching the requested lifecycle point.

B · incorrect — stop suspends activity when deactivated; it is not the post-init startup callback.

C · incorrect — destroy performs cleanup before unloading, rather than starting activity immediately after initialization.

D · incorrect — paint draws content and is not the lifecycle startup callback that follows init.

Question 122

  • C. destroy
  • D. paint

Use the historical host lifecycle and distinguish activation, suspension, drawing and unloading.

Study-guide sections

OOP34 · Legacy applets and lifecycle questions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP34 · Legacy applets and lifecycle questions

Correct answer: C — destroy

The applet lifecycle assigns final cleanup before unloading to destroy. start begins or resumes activity, stop handles host deactivation, and paint draws content. A normal browser shutdown may cause an unload, but unloading can also occur without shutting the browser down. The revised stem therefore asks for the cleanup callback directly and does not make an incorrect exclusive shutdown claim or promise cleanup after an abrupt crash.

Evidence in the complete study note

init initializes once; start follows initialization and resumes activity; stop suspends activity when the host deactivates it; destroy performs final cleanup before unloading. paint draws content and is not a constructor.OOP34
destroy is not defined exclusively as “browser shuts down”: the host may destroy an applet on unloading, and abrupt process termination does not guarantee cleanup.OOP34

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — start begins or resumes activity rather than performing final cleanup.

B · incorrect — stop suspends activity on host deactivation, not final unloading.

C · correct — destroy performs final cleanup before normal applet unloading.

D · incorrect — paint draws content rather than handling final cleanup.

Question 123

What are non-static Java fields declared directly in a class, outside methods, constructors and initializer-block local scopes, called?

  • A. Instance variables
  • B. Local variables
  • C. Class variables
  • D. Static variables

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 35

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Locate the declaration scope and check default initialization versus definite assignment.

Study-guide sections

OOP05 · Variables, defaults, scope and initialization

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP05 · Variables, defaults, scope and initialization

Correct answer: A — Instance variables

Fields belong to a class declaration, but non-static fields hold separate state for each object and are called instance variables. Static fields are class variables shared by instances, so merely being outside a method would not distinguish them. The stem now explicitly excludes static and block-local declarations. Local variables belong to method, constructor or block scopes rather than to each object’s field state.

Evidence in the complete study note

The introductory three-way grouping is local, instance and class/static variables. Locals occur in methods, constructors or blocks; they must be definitely assigned before use and cannot have public/private/protected modifiers. Fields occur in a class outside method bodies; non-static fields belong to each instance, while static fields belong to the class. Declaration location alone does not distinguish instance and static fields.OOP05

Choice by choice

A · correct — Non-static object fields are instance variables.

B · incorrect — Locals belong to executable scopes rather than the class’s object state.

C · incorrect — Class variables are static fields, excluded by the question.

D · incorrect — Static variables are shared class fields, excluded by the question.

Study-guide references

OOP18 · Abstract classes and concrete implementations

Correct answer: C — Used to construct objects

The given class contains an abstract method by assumption, and that method has no implementation body. An abstract class cannot be directly instantiated but can define fields, constructors, abstract methods and concrete methods. It need not contain an abstract method. An abstract method has no body; abstract and final conflict because an operation cannot require overriding while forbidding it.OOP18

A · incorrect — This is true of the particular class because the stem explicitly says it declares an abstract method.

B · incorrect — An abstract method has no implementation body, which is the intended meaning of incomplete.

D · incorrect — C is an incorrect statement, so None of the above cannot be selected.

Question 133

Which listed cases are not checked exceptions in Java? Interpret “array index out of bounds” as ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and “file required not found” as FileNotFoundException. Select all that apply.

  • A. Missing semicolons
  • B. Array index out of bounds
  • C. Usage of undeclared variables
  • D. File required not found

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 110

Study-guide sections

OOP29 · Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP29 · Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

Correct answers (select all): A, B, C — Missing semicolons; Array index out of bounds; Usage of undeclared variables

A missing semicolon and an undeclared variable are source errors rejected during compilation; neither is a checked exception. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is a runtime exception and is unchecked. FileNotFoundException is a checked exception, so its catch-or-declare obligation is checked by the compiler even though an actual throw occurs at runtime. The revised multiple-selection question accepts all three cases outside the checked-exception category.

Evidence in the complete study note

IOException, FileNotFoundException and SQLException are standard checked examples. ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ClassCastException and array bounds exceptions are unchecked. A missing semicolon or undeclared variable is a compile-time source error, not a checked exception.OOP29
Checked does not mean the exception occurs at compile time: the compiler checks an obligation to catch or declare it, while an actual throw occurs at runtime.OOP29

Choice by choice

A · correct — A missing semicolon is a compile-time source error, not a checked exception.

B · correct — ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is unchecked.

C · correct — An undeclared variable is a compile-time source error, not a checked exception.

D · incorrect — FileNotFoundException is checked and therefore is not selected.

B · incorrect — Uses multiple forms within a hierarchy rather than creating its relationship

C · incorrect — Groups data and methods

Question 140

Choose the incorrect statement in terms of Objects.

  • A. Objects are abstractions of real-world
  • B. Objects can't manage themselves
  • C. Objects encapsulate state and representation information
  • D. All of the mentioned

Source

  • Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 88

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Distinguish an object’s stored state, operations, identity and class definition.

Study-guide sections

OOP01 · Objects, classes and responsibilities

OOP02 · Four principles and the difference between hiding and abstraction

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP01 · Objects, classes and responsibilities

OOP02 · Four principles and the difference between hiding and abstraction

Correct answer: B — “Objects cannot manage themselves” is the incorrect generalization.

OOP01 says objects hold state and behavior, control responsibilities, communicate through method calls and can delegate. It expressly calls the claim that objects cannot manage their own state misleading. Therefore B is the false generalization. A is a conventional modeling description, and C describes encapsulated state, so all statements cannot be incorrect.

Evidence in the complete study note

An object has identity, state and behavior. State is stored in fields; behavior is provided by methods. A Rectangle object may hold width and height and answer getArea() or getPerimeter(). Two objects can have equal fields and still be distinct objects. A class defines their common structure and behavior; an object is a particular instance.OOP01
Choose classes around responsibilities: an account controls its own balance, a transaction records a payment, and a service coordinates them. Objects send messages through method calls such as obj.add(). They can delegate work to other objects; saying that objects cannot manage their own state is misleading. Procedural and object oriented designs both support reuse; global shared data is not compulsory in procedural programming.OOP01
Encapsulation groups related state and operations and controls access. Information hiding keeps implementation decisions behind a stable interface. Abstraction presents the essential operations while omitting details irrelevant to the caller.OOP02

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Objects can model abstractions of real-world entities; this conventional modeling description is not the identified false generalization.

B · correct — Objects can control their state through behavior and delegate responsibilities, contradicting this categorical claim.

C · incorrect — Encapsulation of state and related representation is consistent with the note’s object model.

D · incorrect — The supported abstraction and encapsulation descriptions prevent treating every supplied statement as incorrect.

Question 141

Which OOP concept describes one operation in a class hierarchy producing different behavior for different runtime object types?

  • A. Aggregation
  • B. Polymorphism
  • C. Inheritance

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 89

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check what compiles from the declared type, then select behavior from the actual runtime class.

Study-guide sections

OOP15 · Dynamic dispatch: declared type versus actual type

OOP-S05 · Inheritance boundaries and whole-part relationships

OOP02 · Four principles and the difference between hiding and abstraction

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP15 · Dynamic dispatch: declared type versus actual type

OOP-S05 · Inheritance boundaries and whole-part relationships

OOP02 · Four principles and the difference between hiding and abstraction

Correct answer: B — Polymorphism

Polymorphism lets code using a common type invoke behavior appropriate to each concrete object. Eligible overriding supplies this effect at runtime: the same inherited operation may dispatch to a different subclass implementation. Inheritance establishes the relationship that permits those related types, but does not alone name the varying behavior. Aggregation instead models a whole grouping parts, rather than method dispatch.

Evidence in the complete study note

For an eligible overridden sound(), a.sound() invokes Dog.sound() at runtime.OOP15
Aggregation models one instance grouping other instances as a whole with parts. It is an object-relationship concept, not a method-dispatch rule. Inheritance instead relates a specialized class to a general class; overridden operations can then provide polymorphic behavior.OOP-S05
Inheritance forms a subtype relationship and may reuse implementation. Polymorphism lets code using a common type invoke behavior appropriate to different concrete objects.OOP02

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Aggregation describes whole-part object relationships, not varying operation behavior.

B · correct — Polymorphism names behavior selected appropriately for different concrete object types through a common operation.

C · incorrect — Inheritance establishes the subtype hierarchy; polymorphism names the differing behavior through that hierarchy.

Question 142

Which statement correctly describes the implicit object argument in an ordinary C++17 member-function call?

  • A. The this pointer is supplied as the implicit object argument to ordinary non-static member functions
  • B. The this pointer is supplied as a hidden argument to static member variables
  • C. The this pointer is supplied as a hidden argument to static member functions
  • D. The this pointer is supplied as a hidden argument to every member function, including static functions

Adapted from

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 9

OOP17 · C++ this and language-specific assumptions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP17 · C++ this and language-specific assumptions

Correct answer: A — The this pointer is supplied as the implicit object argument to ordinary non-static member functions

In ordinary C++17 non-static member functions, this points to the object on which the function is invoked and can be understood as the implicit object argument. Member variables do not receive call arguments. Static member functions have no current instance and no this pointer, so a claim about every member function is also too broad. Correcting variables to functions in A restores the intended distinction.

Evidence in the complete study note

In ordinary C++17 non-static member functions, this is a pointer to the object on which the function is called; this->field selects a member. It is often explained as an implicit object argument to a member function call. It is not an argument passed to member variables, and a static member function has no this pointer.OOP17

Choice by choice

A · correct — Ordinary non-static member functions have the implicit object represented by this.

B · incorrect — Variables are not calls and do not receive hidden object arguments.

C · incorrect — Static member functions have no this pointer.

D · incorrect — Including static functions makes the universal claim false.

Question 143

What does this Java program print? public class Calculation { public static void main(String[] args) { int sum = 0; for (int j = 1; j <= 10; j++) { sum = sum + j; } System.out.println(+sum); } }

  • A. 55
  • B. 44
  • C. 33
  • D. 66

Adapted from

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 17

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace condition tests, control transfers and printing as separate steps.

Study-guide sections

OOP25 · Control flow traces and exact printing

OOP-S03 · Expression results, assignment and control headers

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP25 · Control flow traces and exact printing

OOP-S03 · Expression results, assignment and control headers

Correct answer: A — 55

The loop adds each integer from 1 through 10 exactly once. Their sum is 10×11/2=55, and unary plus does not change that integer before printing. The malformed trailing token is replaced by the required closing braces, leaving the loop itself unchanged. Forty-four and thirty-three are not the inclusive sum, while sixty-six would correspond to additionally summing 11, beyond the bound.

Evidence in the complete study note

A loop summing j=1..10 yields 55.OOP25
Prefix ++ and -- update a variable before supplying its value; postfix forms supply the old value before the update. Multiplication, division and remainder bind before addition and subtraction; same-level binary arithmetic groups left to right. Integer division truncates toward zero. Unary plus preserves its numeric operand’s value.OOP-S03

Choice by choice

A · correct — The inclusive sum 1+2+…+10 is 55.

B · incorrect — 44 is not the sum of the ten loop values.

C · incorrect — 33 is not the sum produced by the inclusive loop.

D · incorrect — 66 would include an extra 11 beyond the stated upper bound.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

OOP02 · Four principles and the difference between hiding and abstraction

Correct answer: D — Encapsulation controls which information of an object is exposed.

The question specifically asks for the mechanism that groups an object’s state with its operations and controls access to that state. That is encapsulation. Abstraction also matters in the account’s public view, but it names the essential operations presented to callers rather than the requested state-and-operation boundary. Inheritance and polymorphism concern subtype relationships and behavior through common types, respectively.

Encapsulation groups related state and operations and controls access. Information hiding keeps implementation decisions behind a stable interface. These ideas overlap: a private balance plus deposit(amount) can demonstrate all three, depending on what the question emphasizes.OOP02

Question 147

Which most restrictive Java member-access category admits unrelated classes in the same package and qualified subclass access in other packages, while excluding unrelated classes in other packages?

  • A. Public
  • B. Default
  • C. Private
  • D. Protected

Adapted from

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 69

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Locate the accessing code, declaring type, package and receiver before applying visibility rules.

Study-guide sections

OOP08 · Access control and package boundaries

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP08 · Access control and package boundaries

Correct answer: D — Protected, subject to cross-package receiver restrictions.

Protected combines same-package access with qualified subclass access across packages. It therefore reaches both required contexts while excluding unrelated other-package clients. Public is broader and violates that exclusion. Package/default access does not reach the other-package subclass, while private is narrower than the required same-package access. Cross-package instance access must still use the inherited context or an appropriate subclass-typed receiver.

Evidence in the complete study note

For ordinary members: private restricts access to the declaring class/nest; no modifier grants package access; protected grants same-package access plus qualified subclass access; public is widest, provided the declaring type itself is accessible. Top-level classes/interfaces may be public or package-private, not protected/private. Member types have additional visibility possibilities.OOP08
Across packages, a subclass accessing a protected instance member must do so through its own inherited context or an appropriate subclass-typed receiver, not any arbitrary superclass object.OOP08

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Public also admits unrelated classes in other packages, violating the explicit exclusion.

B · incorrect — Package/default access does not admit the required subclass access across packages.

C · incorrect — Private does not grant access to unrelated same-package classes.

D · correct — Protected grants the required same-package and qualified cross-package subclass access without granting universal access.

OOP16 · this, super, fields and static hiding

Correct answer: B — public final double calculateTax(){ return 0.0; }

final explicitly prohibits overriding an instance method while allowing it to remain public and concrete. abstract instead requires an implementation and supplies no body. private would remove public access and create independent child declarations rather than preserve the required public contract. static changes the method into a class operation whose same-signature child method hides it. Only the public final instance declaration satisfies all stated requirements.

final prevents reassignment of a variable, overriding of a method or extension of a class.OOP07

An abstract method has no body; abstract and final conflict because an operation cannot require overriding while forbidding it.OOP18
For ordinary members: private restricts access to the declaring class/nest; no modifier grants package access; protected grants same-package access plus qualified subclass access; public is widest, provided the declaring type itself is accessible.OOP08
Fields are hidden rather than dynamically overridden, and same-signature static methods hide rather than override.OOP16

Question 149

What will be the output for the Java expression: 8 - 2 * 5 * (3 + 9 / 3) + 6 / 3

  • A. -150
  • B. -30
  • C. -50
  • D. 50

Sources

  • National Exit Exam practice questions · Question 1

  • Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 80

Study-guide sections

OOP-S03 · Expression results, assignment and control headers

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP23 · Expressions: numbers, bits and text output

OOP-S03 · Expression results, assignment and control headers

Correct answer: C — -50.

Inside the parentheses, 9/3=3, so the group is 3+3=6. The multiplication gives 2*5*6=60, and the remaining integer division gives 6/3=2. The result is 8-60+2=-50, matching OOP23’s explicit example. The negative sign follows from subtracting the larger product.

Evidence in the complete study note

In 8-2*5*(3+9/3)+6/3, the result is -50.OOP23
Prefix ++ and -- update a variable before supplying its value; postfix forms supply the old value before the update. Multiplication, division and remainder bind before addition and subtraction; same-level binary arithmetic groups left to right. Integer division truncates toward zero. Unary plus preserves its numeric operand’s value.OOP-S03

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — -150 does not follow the parenthesized value 6 and product 60 obtained from the stated operands.

B · incorrect — -30 miscalculates the product or remaining terms; 8-60+2 is -50.

C · correct — The grouped arithmetic gives 8-60+2, which equals -50.

D · incorrect — The product is subtracted, so changing -50 to positive 50 loses the required sign.

An object has identity, state and behavior. State is stored in fields; behavior is provided by methods. A Rectangle object may hold width and height and answer getArea() or getPerimeter().OOP01

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A class groups fields and methods, not just one operation's statements

B · incorrect — Package groups classes/interfaces

C · incorrect — Variable stores data rather than an operation body

D · correct — Matches an operation implemented by a statement body

Question 158

For this valid Java instance method inside a class, which input/output statement is correct? public void test(boolean a, boolean b) { if (a) { System.out.println("A"); } else if (a && b) { System.out.println("A && B"); } else { if (!b) { System.out.println("!B"); } else { System.out.println("None"); } } }

  • A. If a and b are both true, the output is "A && B".
  • B. If a is true and b is false, the output is "!B".
  • C. If a is false and b is true, the output is "None".
  • D. If a and b are both false, the output is "None".

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 76

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace condition tests, control transfers and printing as separate steps.

Study-guide sections

OOP25 · Control flow traces and exact printing

OOP-S03 · Expression results, assignment and control headers

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP25 · Control flow traces and exact printing

OOP-S03 · Expression results, assignment and control headers

Correct answer: C — a=false and b=true prints None.

If a is true, the first branch prints A regardless of b. If a is false, the else-if condition a && b is necessarily false, so execution enters the final else. There !b selects !B when b is false and None when b is true. Only C pairs its input values with the resulting output.

Evidence in the complete study note

In if(a)... else if(a&&b)..., the second condition can never be true on a path reaching it because a is already false.OOP25
For Boolean values, ! reverses true and false, && is true only when both operands are true, and || is true when at least one is true.OOP-S03
An if selects its true branch or, when present, its else branch; only the selected branch executes.OOP-S03

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — When a is true the first branch prints A, not the unreachable A && B branch.

B · incorrect — a=true selects A immediately regardless of b, so !B does not print.

C · correct — a=false bypasses both earlier tests and b=true makes !b false, selecting None.

D · incorrect — With both false, the final !b test is true and prints !B rather than None.

Question 162

Which statements about Java 17 constructors are false? Select all that apply.

  • A. A constructor can be overloaded
  • B. It has the same name as the class
  • C. can be invoked within any method without object instantiation.
  • D. the first line of the constructor must be a call on another constructor in the same class
  • E. Has no return statement

Adapted from

  • Mock exam 1 · Question 21

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check the class name, return-type absence and the constructors actually declared.

Study-guide sections

OOP09 · Constructors and missing default constructors

OOP10 · Constructor chaining and initialization order

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP09 · Constructors and missing default constructors

OOP10 · Constructor chaining and initialization order

Correct answers (select all): C, D, E — can be invoked within any method without object instantiation.; the first line of the constructor must be a call on another constructor in the same class; Has no return statement

Constructors can be overloaded and must use the class’s exact name, so A and B are true. They are not ordinary methods that can be called anywhere without construction. A same-class this(...) call is not mandatory; delegation may use super(...) or implicit super(). Constructors also allow bare return; even though they have no return type and cannot return an expression. Therefore C, D and E are false.

Evidence in the complete study note

A constructor has the class’s exact name and no return type, not even void. It initializes the new object and can be overloaded or private. A private constructor can support a factory or controlled singleton creation; it does not mean the class can never create an object internally.OOP09
Constructors are not inherited or overridden. They may contain return; but cannot return an expression. Fields get their default values before ordinary constructor initialization, rather than receiving defaults only because a default constructor was generated.OOP09
Under Java 17 rules, an explicit this(args) or super(args) invocation must be the first constructor statement. this invokes another constructor in the same class; super invokes the immediate superclass constructor. A constructor cannot explicitly invoke both. If there is no explicit delegation, an implicit super() is inserted; a matching accessible no-argument parent constructor must exist.OOP10

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Overloading constructors is permitted, so this statement is true.

B · incorrect — A constructor has the exact class name, so this statement is true.

C · correct — Constructors are not ordinary methods callable from any method without construction.

D · correct — An explicit same-class constructor call is not mandatory.

E · correct — A bare return; is allowed, so the claim of no return statement is false.

  • B. drive: brake hard
  • C. generic nose: drive: brake hard

OOP21 · Casts and instanceof

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

OOP21 · Casts and instanceof

Correct answer: E — Runtime ClassCastException before any drive or brake output.

a refers to an actual Car created with new Car(), not to a Ferrari. The cast is type-checkable because Ferrari is a subclass, but it fails at runtime as OOP21 states. Execution stops at the cast with ClassCastException, before a.drive() or d.brake() can print any of their messages.

Evidence in the complete study note

Upcasting a subclass reference to a superclass is implicit and does not change the object. A downcast may pass compile-time type checks yet fail at runtime. Car a=new Car(); Ferrari f=(Ferrari)a; throws ClassCastException before subsequent drive() or brake() calls. It does not turn a plain Car into a Ferrari.OOP21

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — The failing cast occurs before either drive or brake, so neither listed message prints.

B · incorrect — No Ferrari object exists here; the cast throws before any dynamic drive or brake call.

C · incorrect — The program never reaches any of the three proposed messages because the cast fails first.

D · incorrect — The related-class cast can pass compile-time checking; the actual object type causes a runtime failure.

E · correct — Casting a plain Car object to Ferrari throws ClassCastException at runtime before any method output.

  • B. int [ ] x, y = new int[5];

OOP05 · Variables, defaults, scope and initialization

Correct answers (select all): B, D — int [ ] x, y = new int[5];; int [ ] x = new int[4];

In B, int[] is the shared type of both x and y. Only y receives a new five-element array, which is a legal declaration as long as unassigned x is not read. Thus B and D are valid.

int[] a=new int[5]; and int a[]={1,2,3}; are valid. int[] a={}; creates a zero-length array; explicit new is unnecessary in a declaration initializer. int a[],b; makes only a an array; int[] c,d; makes both arrays. Locals occur in methods, constructors or blocks; they must be definitely assigned before use and cannot have public/private/protected modifiers.OOP05

Study-guide references

OOP07 · Static members, static blocks and final

Correct answer: A — A block that initializes class-level state during class initialization, before that class’s first relevant active use, including its main invocation

A static initializer executes during class initialization and can initialize static state. It runs before the class’s first relevant active use, including invoking its main method, rather than simply whenever a class file is loaded. It is a real Java construct, so none and the denial option are false. Synchronization is a different concern and does not define a static initializer’s purpose.
